turns.replyText:
Can you explain the main options in simple terms?

Absolutely, I can break it down simply. When you’re choosing a rose, these are the main options to think about:

Shape of the plant (how it grows)
Shrub/bush roses: Look like a rounded bush. Great for most gardens and “easy first roses.” Good for flower beds and borders.
Climbing roses: Long canes you tie to an arch, fence, trellis, or wall. Perfect if you want a covered arch or a wall of flowers.
Groundcover / landscape roses: Low and spreading. Good for covering a slope or the front of a bed.
Hybrid tea roses: Tall, elegant plants with big classic “florist-style” blooms, usually one bloom per stem. Best if you want long stems for vases.
Floribunda roses: Lots of blooms in clusters. Slightly smaller flowers than hybrid teas, but many more at once, very showy.
Size Every rose on our site lists a height and width in feet, not inches.
Smaller (around 2–3 feet): Good for pots or the front of a bed.
Medium (3–5 feet): Most common and versatile.
Large or climbing (5+ feet tall or tall with long canes): Good for fences, walls, pergolas, and back of borders.
Sun needs
Full sun: 6 or more hours of direct sunlight each day. Most roses are happiest here.
Partial shade: At least 4 hours of sun; these areas are more shade tolerant. Many roses can still do well as long as they get those 4+ hours.
Bloom style and timing
Repeat blooming: Blooms, rests, then blooms again through the season.
Continuous blooming: Keeps blooming almost nonstop during the season, with only short breaks.
Once-blooming: One big flush of flowers, usually in late spring or early summer, then mainly green the rest of the year.
Fragrance and care level
Some roses are highly fragrant but may need a bit more attention.
Others are more disease-resistant and low-maintenance, great if you want something easier with less fuss.
How we ship
All our roses are own-root and come in 1-gallon containers with soil. They are defoliated before shipping, so they often arrive without leaves or buds. They leaf out once they settle into your garden.

turns.replyText:
How do I use it properly the very first time?

Great question. I’ll walk you through using the Get Growing Bundle the first time when you plant.

First, are you planting in the ground or in a container? I’ll give quick directions for both:

If you’re planting in the ground Use everything as you prepare the planting hole.
Dig the hole
Dig about 2 feet wide and deep enough so the rose will sit at the same level it was in its pot (not deeper).
Aged cow manure
Put a few inches of your regular soil in the bottom of the hole.
Mix some aged cow manure into that bottom area (a few handfuls around the base area is plenty for one rose).
Bone meal
In a bucket or wheelbarrow, mix the soil you dug out with bone meal.
For one rose, about 1 cup of bone meal mixed into that soil is a good first-time amount.
Mint compost
Mix some mint compost into that same soil mix.
You can also save some to spread on top of the soil after planting as a “top dressing” around the plant.
Plant the rose
Put some of your amended soil (soil + bone meal + mint compost) back into the hole on top of the manure layer.
Set the rose in the hole so it sits at the same height as in its pot.
Fill in around it with the amended soil and press down gently to remove air pockets.
Water deeply.
Founders Fish Fertilizer (liquid)
Mix 4 oz of fish fertilizer into 1 gallon of water (check the cap or label; 4 oz is about half a cup).
Slowly pour this around the base of the rose after planting.
For the first year, you can repeat this every 4–6 weeks during the growing season.
If you’re planting in a container Same products, just slightly different use.
Prepare the pot
Use a pot at least 10–15 gallons for a bush rose.
Make sure it has drainage holes.
Aged cow manure
Mix some cow manure into your potting soil before you fill the container (about 1 part manure to 3–4 parts potting soil is plenty).
Bone meal
Add about 1 cup of bone meal into that potting soil mix and stir it in well.
Plant the rose
Put some of this mixed soil in the bottom.
Set the rose so it sits at the same level it was in its original pot.
Fill around it with your amended soil and press gently.
Mint compost
Spread a layer of mint compost on top of the soil around the rose as a mulch (this helps keep moisture in and protects roots).
Founders Fish Fertilizer
Mix 4 oz per gallon of water.
Water the rose with this mix after planting.
For container roses, you can repeat every 3–4 weeks during the growing season.

That’s all you need for the very first use: mix cow manure and bone meal into the planting soil, use mint compost in the soil and as a top layer, and water in with diluted fish fertilizer.
